tagline.text: Natural rock pools on Siargao's east coast that appear only at low tide

location.label: Location
location.text: Magpupungko Beach, Pilar, Siargao Island, Surigao del Norte

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: March–October (possible in the rainy season when the tide timing fits)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300–1,000 (general entry, scooter rental and meals, per day)

children.text: Magpupungko Rock Pools are limestone tidal pools on the Pilar coast of eastern Siargao, where a clear natural swimming pool sheltered from the sea appears only at low tide. Entry is about ₱50 and the pools are about 45 minutes by scooter from General Luna, so if the tide is right, cliff jumping and beachside restaurants make for a half-day that is a Siargao must-do.

Magpupungko Rock Pools are on the east coast of Siargao Island, in front of Magpupungko Beach in the municipality of Pilar, Surigao del Norte. A limestone reef shields the area from big ocean waves, so at low tide a clear, calm natural swimming pool appears behind it. When the tide comes in, the pools disappear under seawater and waves roll over the rocks. That is why any plan here starts with the tide.

The name is said to come from the Visayan word pungko, "to squat," because of a large rock near the pools that looks as if it is sitting on another rock. The spelling also appears as Magpopongko. The pools range from shallow lagoons to deep areas about
deep. The big rock in the middle is used as a cliff-jumping spot, and around the headland there are smaller pools and rocks with fewer people.
It is about
35 km
from General Luna, roughly
45 minutes

by scooter, and you reach it by following the island's circumferential road toward Pilar. It is often presented as part of a land tour together with Tayangban Cave Pool, Coconut Road, the Maasin River rope swing and the Palm Tree Viewpoint near Pilar.

The entrance fee is known to be about ₱50–60 per person and is described as an environmental fee. Sources differ slightly on the amount, and some say it is free, so confirm at the entrance. The beach has small restaurants, coconut stalls, and paid showers and toilets, which makes it a good place to stay for half a day. A guide is not required, and you can explore on your own. Opening hours and fees are described differently by different sources, so check the latest information locally.

blocks.title: Natural pools that appear at low tide

children.text: The highlight of Magpupungko is seeing clear turquoise pools emerge inside the limestone reef. You can float in the shallow edges and swim in the deep middle. You can also see the rock bed, small caves and fish underwater. When the sun is high the water is clear enough to see coral fragments and rock on the bottom. Many people rent life jackets and snorkeling gear, so even weaker swimmers can enjoy it safely.

blocks.title: Cliff jumping from the big rock

children.text: A large rock stands in the middle of the first pool and is used as the jumping spot. Sources describe it as about 3–5 m high, so it is not very high. The depth changes with the tide, so always check the depth before you jump. The water at the jumping spot is known to be about
deep, but even the same spot varies with the water level, so it is safest to get in and check first. Look first to see who else is in the water before you copy the locals and surfers who jump.
About
around the headland from the big pool there are smaller pools and a large rock. It is quiet with fewer people, but because waves come in from that side, you must respect the tide.

blocks.title: Heart-shaped rock and coastal rock beds

children.text: The large rock in the middle of the first pool is described as heart-shaped. Walking across the rock beds and photographing the shore landscape revealed after the water recedes is also rewarding.

Right next to the pools is a long beach of mixed sand and reef. At low tide it is rocky, and at high tide the sand is submerged and swimming improves, so many people advise enjoying the pools at low tide and the beach at high tide.
Small restaurants line the beach in the shade of palm trees, selling Filipino home cooking such as adobo and curry, plus coconut juice. It is a nice place to wait for the tide in a hammock.

blocks.title: Tayangban Cave Pool and Palm Tree Road

children.text: On the way toward Pilar there are Tayangban Cave Pool, Coconut Road and the Palm Tree Viewpoint, so it is easy to combine them on the same day. The cave pool is known as an experience of floating in darkness with a torch.

items.title: Half day timed to low tide
items.subtitle: From General Luna to Magpupungko

children.text: The day before, check the tide chart for Pilar to decide the low-tide time. Set your departure so that you arrive 1–2 hours before low tide.
Ride a scooter from General Luna and head north along the island's circumferential road. It takes about
45 minutes
, and on the way you pass the signs for Tayangban Cave Pool. Follow the road signs to the access road.
At the entrance hut, pay the entrance fee (about
) and the parking fee, and get your water shoes and dry bag ready.
Walk a few minutes along the coastal path from the beach to the pools. When the tide starts to fall, the pools are revealed.
Swim and jump from the big rock for about an hour around low tide. This time of day also has good morning light for photos.
Leave the pools before the water rises. Have lunch and rest at a beach restaurant.
On the way back, stop at Tayangban Cave Pool or Palm Tree Road.
Low tide shifts by more than an hour every day. Always check the tide chart for your date.
Start a land tour from General Luna. When booking, check that the itinerary includes Magpupungko.
Head toward Pilar and stop at Coconut Road and the viewpoint.
Enter Magpupungko and swim.
Have lunch at a beach restaurant and head back.

Tours differ by operator in the stops they include and in price, so when you book, check that the Magpupungko visit time matches the low tide. If the tour schedule does not match the tide, there are days when you cannot see the pools.
There are flights from Manila Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL) to Siargao Sayak Airport (IAO). Check the airline's announcements for routes and schedules.
You can also go via Cebu and other places. Operations change by season, so check when you book.
From the airport to General Luna, take a shared van, taxi or habal-habal (motorcycle taxi). Check the fare locally.
It is about
35 km
and about
45 minutes
from General Luna, and a scooter gives you the most freedom. A day's rental is described as about
The road is generally well paved, but be careful on rainy days and after dark.
When you see the access road sign, turn right and park your motorbike in front of the entrance hut.

When renting, make sure you have a helmet and a license, and check the fuel and tires. The road toward Pilar is lined with palm trees and is scenic, but it is dark after sunset, so return before dark.
From General Luna you can hire a habal-habal, or take a multicab or van heading north, tell them to drop you off at Magpupungko, and walk in.
Land tours and rented vans combine the pools with Tayangban Cave Pool, Coconut Road and more. Prices and inclusions differ by operator, so compare them and confirm locally.

At Magpupungko, the tide matters more than the season. In any month you can see the pools if you go at low tide, and when the tide is in, swimming is dangerous, so entry may be restricted. The usual advice is to arrive 1–2 hours before low tide and enjoy about an hour on either side of it.
The most stable weather is known to be
March–October
. Siargao tends to have rain and waves in
November–February
, so check sea conditions. Midday is crowded, so it is better to go early in the morning.

Low tide moves by more than an hour every day. On the same itinerary, low tide may come at dawn one day and at midday on another, so when you fit Magpupungko into your Siargao plans, choose a day when low tide falls in the morning. Check the tide chart for Pilar (Port Pilar); a low tide around sunrise gives the best light and fewer people.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: Best if low tide is in the morning; midday is very hot
The sea may be cloudy after rain; tide comes first
If waves are high the pools are dangerous, so check locally

items.note: Per person, includes Magpupungko Beach; varies by source

items.note: Cars may pay a little more

There are lodgings in Pilar near Magpupungko, but most travelers stay in General Luna and make a half-day or full-day trip. General Luna has everything from guesthouses to resorts, and plenty of restaurants and cafes.

Small restaurants and coconut stalls line Magpupungko Beach under the palm trees. You can eat Filipino home cooking such as adobo, curry and rice, and some shop names are mentioned online, but they change often, so choose on the spot. There are no lockers, so leave valuables behind.

The beach restaurants are the closest place to eat. There are a few under the palms, and lunch is generally said to cost within a few hundred pesos, but confirm menus and prices locally. A little farther away there is also a cafe known for chicken adobo and vegetable curry. On days when low tide is early in the morning, restaurants may open late, so it is safer to bring water and a light snack. Paid showers and toilets are said to be available; check the fees locally.
The day before, check the tide chart for Pilar and arrive 1–2 hours before low tide.
Water shoes are essential. The rocks are sharp and slippery, so going barefoot or in sandals is risky.
Bring a dry bag. You have to leave your things near the entrance, and there are no lockers.
Swim to check the depth before you jump. The depth varies with the water level.
It is crowded at midday, so going early in the morning is quieter.
When renting a scooter, have an international driving permit and a helmet.
Fees and rules can change locally, so check at the entrance hut.
Put your phone in a waterproof case or leave it behind when you go to the pools. It is safer to ask a companion to take jump photos from the beach.
The beach is better at high tide, so plan to enjoy the pools first and then rest on the beach once the water rises.
After low tide ends, the water rises quickly and waves roll over the rocks. As soon as the tide starts to come in, get out of the pools right away.
At high tide, waves surge into the pools and swimming is dangerous. Entry may be restricted for safety at high water.
The sharp rocks cut easily. Some places around the pools also have strong currents, so hold on to the rocks as you move.
The pools are reported to be about
from the beach, so you must cross shallow sea to reach them. Come back toward the beach before the water rises, and if you went to the far beach, leave before high tide arrives.
Around noon the crowds make the jumping spot busy. Check who is in the water before you jump.
Do not bring valuables, or put them in a dry bag. There is no storage.
Siargao
, where Magpupungko lies, is famous for surfing and island tours, and many tours depart from General Luna.
A cave pool on the way toward Pilar, where you float for about
15 minutes
in the dark by torchlight and, at the end, there is reportedly a cliff jump of about
7 m

blocks.title: Palm Tree Viewpoint and Coconut Road

children.text: A road lined with palm trees and a viewpoint, known as a photo spot for sunrise and sunset.
A river with a coconut tree rope swing that is often included in land tours.
A beach reached from the same coastal road as Magpupungko, with paid shades and chairs for rent in some places. It is a good stop while you wait for the tide at Magpupungko.
